archetype.name: Rebuilding (pass defense in freefall)
archetype.definition: A first-year staff with a functional, ball-control offense, attached to a pass defense that ranks near the bottom of the league in every coverage measure, and now missing two starting linemen.

report.headline: A competent offense can't outrun a secondary that gives up everything.
report.take:
Arizona's 1-4 is an honest record. The point differential of -10.8 a game ranks 31st, and wins over expected sit at only -0.65. Turnover margin is dead even. This isn't a team losing coin flips. It loses by multiple scores: 24 to Seattle, 12 to the Giants as a favorite, 24 to Detroit. The one win came at the Chargers, whose offense now ranks 32nd. Mike LaFleur inherits a franchise that won three games last year and four in two of the three seasons before that, and nothing here says the cycle is broken yet.

The split is stark. The offense is average, not bad: 17th in EPA and 10th in success rate, with Jacoby Brissett keeping the chains moving and the ball for over 31 minutes a game. Trey McBride (56 targets) and Michael Wilson (51) carry the passing game. Jeremiyah Love takes the lead-back carries with Tyler Allgeier behind him. What the offense lacks is big plays: pass EPA is 21st. The defense is the problem. Opponents throw on it at 0.362 EPA per dropback (31st), hit explosive passes more often than against anyone in the league (32nd), and beat it deep (30th) and short (31st) alike. Over the last four games it has allowed 31, 36, 36 and 45 points.

The numbers hide a few things. The run defense grades well (11th in rush EPA allowed) and the tackling is clean (6th in missed-tackle rate). That points to a coverage and pass-rush problem, not effort or fundamentals. Opponents don't need to run because the air is wide open, although Seattle and Detroit still ran for 162 and 163 when they chose to. The offensive line looked like a quiet strength: 12th in pressure allowed and the fewest line penalties. That changed this month. Left tackle Paris Johnson Jr. (100% of snaps) is on IR for the season, and guard Isaiah Adams is out until November. The Detroit game, with five sacks allowed, may be a preview.

The direction is down. The defense is getting worse, not stabilizing. The secondary is now missing safety Andrew Wingard, with Wydett Williams questionable after a concussion. The line protecting a quarterback with no downfield game just lost its anchor. The schedule has soft spots: Washington, Philadelphia, New Orleans and the Jets are all at home or beatable. A four-to-six win season is the realistic band, with the 2026 priority being to find out which defensive pieces are worth keeping.

strengths.title: Run defense and tackling hold up
strengths.body: Arizona allows -0.143 EPA per rush (11th) and misses tackles on just 5.7% of attempts (6th). The front plays its gaps and finishes plays, so the leaks are in coverage rather than effort. This should hold. It only matters, though, when opponents choose to run.

strengths.title: Offense that stays on schedule
strengths.body: A 45.8% success rate (10th), 80% short-yardage conversion (7th) and over 31 minutes of possession (10th) show an offense that sustains drives and shortens games. It is built on Brissett distributing to McBride and Wilson rather than on big plays. That keeps games closer than the defense deserves, but it has a ceiling.

strengths.title: McBride as a true focal point
strengths.body: McBride's 56 targets lead the team and anchor a passing game that funnels to its tight end and top wideout. The concentration makes Arizona predictable, but it gives Brissett a reliable answer on money downs. Marvin Harrison Jr. has only 13 targets in four games, so there is no secondary source of volume.

concerns.title: Pass defense broken at every depth
concerns.body: Arizona ranks 31st in pass EPA allowed, 32nd in explosive pass rate allowed, 30th on deep throws and 31st on short ones. Opposing WR1s average 0.87 EPA per target, the worst in the league. A 22nd-ranked pressure rate means quarterbacks are comfortable. Now two safeties are hurt. This is a structural flaw that gets worse before it gets better.

concerns.title: Line just lost its left tackle
concerns.body: Paris Johnson Jr. played every snap before going on season-ending IR, and guard Isaiah Adams (81% of snaps) is out until November. The line ranked 12th in pressure allowed with its starters in place. Detroit got home five times in the first game of the reshuffle. With an offense that wins on rhythm, not explosives, extra pressure kills drives.

concerns.title: Red zone and special teams bleed points
concerns.body: Opponents score touchdowns on 76.5% of red-zone trips (28th), turning drives that stall elsewhere into sevens. Special teams cost 2.33 EPA a game (25th). Together they explain how a defense ranked 26th in yards allowed is dead last in points allowed.

trend.note: The road win at the Chargers has been followed by four losses, three of them by 12 or more. Points allowed have climbed from 31 to 36 to 36 to 45, and the offensive line lost two starters going into Week 6.

nextGame.headline: Rams' coverage takes away exactly what Arizona throws to
nextGame.body:
The Rams are better than 2-3. Their net EPA ranks 7th, they lead the league in yards per game, and they are 1.13 wins under expectation. Their defense lines up badly for Arizona: 1st in deep EPA allowed, 2nd against tight ends, 4th against WR1s. That is McBride and Wilson, who account for most of Brissett's volume. The opening is underneath. The Rams give RBs 23.7% of targets against a league share of 18.2%, and WR3s have found room (31st in PPR over average), so Love and Kendrick Bourne may be where yards come from. On the other side, a Rams offense that passes well above expectation (5th) with a line allowing pressure only 13.5% of the time (3rd) faces the league's worst explosive-pass defense. Stafford should have time all afternoon.

Availability tilts the same way. Arizona's patched line, without Johnson and Adams, does catch a break: the Rams rank 27th in QB hit rate and 25th in sacks, and Myles Garrett remains on IR and isn't expected back this week. The Cardinals' secondary is thinner, with Wingard out and Williams questionable after a concussion. The Rams' own weaknesses are their 32nd-ranked special teams and a habit of not turning yards into points (23.8 a game on 425 yards). Those are the only real paths to a backdoor cover.

keyMatchups.title: Stafford against the league's leakiest secondary
keyMatchups.body: The Rams pass more than expected and protect well. Arizona can't generate pressure and allows the most explosive passes in the league. Missing a safety or two makes it worse. This is the matchup that decides whether the Rams hit 30.

keyMatchups.title: McBride versus a TE-stingy defense
keyMatchups.body: The Rams allow -0.23 EPA per target to tight ends (2nd) and lead the league against deep throws. Arizona's offense runs through McBride. If he is bottled up, Brissett has to win with Love underneath, and that is a slower, lower-scoring path.

keyMatchups.title: Rams' special teams as an equalizer
keyMatchups.body: Los Angeles gives away 5.55 EPA a game on special teams, the worst in the league. That and a red-zone defense ranked 22nd are why a team averaging 425 yards scores under 24 points. Arizona needs field position and short fields to stay inside two touchdowns.

nextGame.watch: Whether Arizona's backup left tackle holds up well enough for Brissett to find Love and the third receiver underneath, since the Rams take away the deep ball and McBride.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense should stay in the low 20s against average defenses. It is efficient enough to sustain drives, and its volume is concentrated in McBride and Wilson. Losing Johnson for the year shaves some of that, especially against the better fronts (Seattle, Denver, the Jets). The defense is the variable. Its run defense and tackling are real, but nothing in its pressure or coverage numbers suggests the pass defense rebounds to average. The 32.4 points allowed per game should ease slightly as the schedule softens with Washington, Philadelphia and New Orleans. It won't approach league average.

The remaining schedule has six or so games where Arizona can be competitive: Washington, Philadelphia and the Jets at home, the trip to New Orleans, Las Vegas, and Dallas, whose defense ranks 32nd. It also has a closing stretch with two Seattle and Rams games, Kansas City and San Francisco. Turnover margin is neutral and close-game luck is only slightly negative, so there's little positive regression owed. Expect three to five more wins.
swingFactors: Whether the reshuffled line protects Brissett without Johnson
Safety health and any pass-rush improvement
Harrison Jr. becoming a real third option

bets.reason: The Rams rank 2nd against tight ends and 4th against WR1s, which is where Arizona's volume goes. They also lead the league against deep passes, and Arizona's line just lost its left tackle. Arizona scored 7 against the one elite defense it has faced, and Detroit sacked Brissett five times in the first game without Johnson.

Two touchdowns is a lot to lay for a 2-3 team with a -0.2 point differential. The Rams score 23.8 a game despite leading the league in yards and have the league's worst special teams. Arizona's ball-control offense (10th in time of possession) shortens games. The edge is modest, because Arizona's defense has allowed 36+ in three of four.

confidence.note: Five games and a new staff. The pass-defense collapse is consistent, but the offensive line injuries change the offense's baseline from here.
